text.en: Raju saw a fossil of a shell in a museum. "That shows life of long ago," said his teacher.

Evidence suggests life existed on Earth at least 3.5 billion years ago. The exact date when it began remains uncertain. Evidences for evolution come from fossils, comparative anatomy and embryology. Lamarck's theory said that organs used more are developed and passed on, while Darwin and Wallace explained how inherited traits that affect survival and reproduction can change a population across generations.
Variation is the difference among individuals of the same species, and it is the raw material for natural selection. Palaeobotany is the study of fossil plants, and fossilisation is how remains are preserved in rocks, and radiometric dating can estimate the age of suitable associated rocks.
Ethnobotany studies how people use plants, and astrobiology or exobiology looks for life beyond Earth.
Evidence suggests life was present on Earth at least three and a half billion years ago. The exact date when life first arose is uncertain.
Evidences for evolution come from fossils, comparative anatomy and embryology.

Lamarck proposed that changes from use or disuse could be inherited. Darwin and Wallace explained how inherited traits that affect survival and reproduction can become more common through natural selection.
Variation is the difference among individuals in a population. When those differences are inherited and affect reproductive success, natural selection can change the population over generations.
Palaeobotany studies fossil plants. Fossilisation preserves some remains or traces of earlier organisms. Radiometric dating can estimate the age of suitable rocks associated with fossils.
Ethnobotany studies how people use plants, and astrobiology or exobiology looks for life beyond Earth.
The origin of life asks how the earliest living systems arose. Evolution asks how heritable features of populations change over generations.

board.text: Origin and evolution ask different questions

text.en: Scientists compare hypotheses with evidence from ancient rocks, fossils and chemistry. Many details about the first living systems remain uncertain.

board.text: Early-life explanations are tested against evidence

text.en: A shell, a leaf impression or a footprint can give evidence of earlier life. A footprint is a trace of an organism’s activity.

board.text: Fossils can be remains or traces

text.en: Rapid burial can protect some remains or traces from being scattered. Hard parts such as bones or shells are often more likely to survive.
Minerals may fill spaces or replace parts of buried remains. A fossil can keep details of the original shape without retaining the original material.
Most organisms leave no fossil. A missing example in a rock layer does not by itself prove that the organism was absent.
In a sedimentary sequence that has not been overturned, deeper layers usually formed earlier than layers above them.

board.text: Undisturbed lower layers are generally older

text.en: Rock layers can place events in order. Radiometric dating can provide a numerical estimate from suitable minerals or nearby datable layers.
Fossil leaves, pollen and wood can help scientists reconstruct past vegetation and environments.

board.text: Palaeobotany studies evidence of earlier plants

text.en: A human arm and a whale flipper have related bones arranged in a similar order, though they have different jobs.

board.text: Homologous structures share an underlying plan

text.en: A bird wing and an insect wing both serve flight, but their basic structures differ. Similar functions alone do not establish a close relationship.
Comparisons of developmental stages can reveal similarities. Scientists check those patterns alongside evidence from anatomy, fossils and other sources.

board.text: Related organisms may share developmental features

text.en: A reduced feature can reveal an ancestral structure. Some reduced structures still have a present-day function.
Lamarck proposed that use or disuse could alter structures and that the change would pass to offspring. This account is different from natural selection.
Training can strengthen a person’s muscles. Their children do not inherit those trained muscles, though they can inherit other features.

board.text: An acquired change usually is not inherited

text.en: Imagine beetles in two inherited colours. Before the environment changes, both colours are already present in the population.
On dark ground, darker beetles may be less visible to predators. If more of them reproduce, more offspring may inherit their colour.
Individual beetles do not change colour to suit the ground. The fraction of each inherited colour can change from one generation to the next.
If the background becomes light, a colour that was less visible on dark ground might be easier to see. A helpful feature can lose its advantage.
Survival matters when it helps individuals leave offspring. The difference that can shift inherited traits is a difference in reproductive success.

board.text: Selection concerns reproduction as well as survival

text.en: Useful inherited traits are not produced because an organism needs them. Existing variation and conditions influence which individuals leave offspring.

board.text: Evolution does not follow a planned goal

text.en: Researchers can learn how communities have used plants for food, fibres or other purposes. This is different from studying fossil plants.

board.text: Ethnobotany studies relationships between people and plants

text.en: Water and other conditions can be clues to whether a place might support life. A clue to habitability is not proof that life is present.

board.text: Astrobiology studies habitability and possible life beyond Earth

text.en: Fossils help place change in time. Anatomy and development help identify shared patterns, and natural selection explains one way inherited features can spread.

board.text: Compare explanations using several kinds of evidence

problem.en: Which two naturalists independently developed the idea of natural selection?

text.en: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently developed the idea.

why.en: They explained how inherited variation and differences in reproduction can change populations over generations.

problem.en: Two fossils occur in different layers of undisturbed sedimentary rock. Which is generally older?

text.en: Find the layer containing each fossil.

why.en: The two layers preserve evidence from different times.

text.en: The fossil in the lower layer is usually older.

why.en: In an undisturbed sequence, earlier sediments lie below later sediments.

problem.en: Why are a human arm and a whale flipper described as homologous?

text.en: Compare the arrangement of their bones.

why.en: They have a shared basic structural plan.

text.en: The same broad plan has been modified for different uses.

why.en: Homology points to shared ancestry rather than identical function.

problem.en: An inherited dark colour makes beetles harder to see on dark ground. What might happen over generations?

text.en: Darker beetles may survive and leave more offspring.

why.en: The advantage depends on local conditions.

text.en: Dark colour can become more common among descendants.

why.en: The population changes when some inherited traits are passed on more often.

prompt.en: A friend says Lamarck proposed natural selection. How will you reply?

points.en: Darwin and Wallace independently developed explanations of natural selection.
Natural selection acts on inherited variation that affects reproductive success.
Astrobiology looks for life in space.
